title: Electromagnetic spectrum and wavelength ranges
prior_knowledge_summary: Every electromagnetic wave is transverse and travels at c in free space.
For electromagnetic waves in free space, c = f lambda, so higher frequency means shorter wavelength.
new_learning: Order radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays by wavelength and frequency.
Recall useful approximate free-space wavelength ranges, including the 400 to 700 nm visible range.
not_yet_taught: Polarisation as evidence of transverse waves.

blocks.heading: One signal family, very different jobs
content: A radio telescope and an X-ray scanner both detect electromagnetic waves. Why can one wavelength cross a room as a broadcast while another reveals bones?
The family is ordered by wavelength or frequency. Locating a wave in that order is the first step towards recognising its region.

figure.purpose: Create a need to organise electromagnetic waves by scale.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch. Place a radio telescope, warm hand, eye and simple X-ray screen along one unlabeled wavelength arrow. Use sparse question marks so the order is not yet revealed.
figure.alt_text: Several electromagnetic-wave applications wait to be placed on a wavelength scale.

blocks.heading: Build the spectrum from long to short
content: From longest wavelength to shortest, the principal regions are radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays.
The frequency order is reversed. Gamma rays have the highest frequency and radio waves the lowest because c = f lambda and c is fixed in free space.
A useful memory path is to rebuild the sequence from its two ends and then fill the middle, rather than remembering a sentence without meaning.

figure.purpose: Make the opposite wavelength and frequency directions explicit.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper spectrum ribbon. Show the seven named regions from radio to gamma. Put a long-to-short wavelength arrow above and a low-to-high frequency arrow below. Keep widths schematic, not proportional.
figure.alt_text: The seven electromagnetic regions run from radio to gamma as wavelength decreases and frequency increases.

blocks.heading: Use approximate boundary landmarks
content: Spectrum boundaries are approximate, so learn scale landmarks rather than pretending that nature changes sharply at one exact value.

A useful free-space map in metres is: radio longer than about 10^-1 m; microwaves about 10^-3 to 10^-1 m; infrared about 7 x 10^-7 to 10^-3 m; visible about 4 x 10^-7 to 7 x 10^-7 m; ultraviolet about 10^-8 to 4 x 10^-7 m; X-rays about 10^-11 to 10^-8 m; gamma rays shorter than about 10^-11 m.
Neighbouring conventions may overlap slightly. In an exam, the region and sensible order of magnitude matter more than a false exact boundary.

figure.purpose: Anchor each region to an approximate power-of-ten wavelength range.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper logarithmic ruler from 10^1 m to 10^-13 m. Add coloured brackets for the seven regions and label boundaries as approximate. Make overlap at neighbouring boundaries visually acceptable.
figure.alt_text: A logarithmic wavelength ruler gives approximate metre ranges for all seven electromagnetic regions.

blocks.heading: Classify from a wavelength
content: Suppose a free-space wave has wavelength 3.0 x 10^-5 m. First compare its power of ten with the boundary landmarks.
The value lies between about 7 x 10^-7 m and 10^-3 m, so it is infrared radiation.
Check the order: 3.0 x 10^-5 m is shorter than typical microwaves but longer than visible light. Both comparisons support the classification.

figure.purpose: Model classification by bracketing a wavelength between two landmarks.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked number-line sketch. Mark 10^-3 m, 3.0 x 10^-5 m and 7 x 10^-7 m, bracket infrared, then add short arrows towards microwave and visible neighbours.
figure.alt_text: A wavelength of three times ten to the minus five metres is bracketed inside the infrared range.

blocks.heading: Convert frequency before classifying
content: A wave is given by frequency 6.0 x 10^14 Hz. Use the formula to remember from the previous lesson, v = f lambda, with v = c in free space.
Five hundred nanometres lies between 400 nm and 700 nm, so the wave is visible. Multiplying 6.0 x 10^14 Hz by 5.0 x 10^-7 m returns 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1, which independently checks the conversion.

figure.purpose: Connect frequency conversion, nanometres and visible-range classification.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper four-step worked layout: rearrange, substitute, convert 5.0 x 10^-7 m to 500 nm, place 500 nm inside a 400 to 700 nm bracket, then show the product check.
figure.alt_text: A frequency calculation gives 500 nanometres, which lies within the visible range.

blocks.heading: Two arrows, not one
content: It is easy to learn the region names correctly and then attach the wrong direction. The mistake feels natural because higher often sounds like bigger.
Higher frequency does not mean longer wavelength in free space. Since c is constant, raising f makes lambda smaller.
Another trap is treating 400 to 700 nm as an exact colour boundary shared by every observer and convention. It is the approximate free-space range visible to the human eye that this course requires.

figure.purpose: Correct reversed ordering and false precision at spectrum boundaries.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper error clinic. Cross out parallel frequency and wavelength arrows, replace them with opposite arrows, and show 400 to 700 nm inside a softly edged visible bracket labelled approximate.
figure.alt_text: Frequency rises as wavelength falls, and the visible range is shown with approximate boundaries.

blocks.heading: A reliable spectrum routine
content: First decide whether the given quantity is wavelength or frequency. If needed, use c = f lambda to convert it.
Next place the value on a power-of-ten wavelength scale. Then name the region and check that its neighbours make sense.
Remember the full long-to-short order: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, ultraviolet, X-ray, gamma. Visible light occupies approximately 400 to 700 nm in free space.

figure.purpose: Unify ordering, conversion and classification into one decision route.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper flow map: identify given quantity, convert if needed with c equals f lambda, locate power of ten, name region, check neighbours. Add the seven-region order and a small 400 to 700 nm visible inset.
figure.alt_text: A decision route converts and locates a wave before naming its electromagnetic region.

misconceptions_addressed: Spectrum boundaries are exact universal cutoffs.
Visible light extends outside approximately 400 to 700 nm in free space.
